awd_titl_txt: CIVIC-PG Track A:  Sustainable Biochar to Mitigate Freshwater HABs: Building Climate Resilient Rural Communities
awd_abstract_narration:
Lakes worldwide are impacted by harmful algal blooms (HABs), also known as cyanoHABs. HABs can lower water quality and produce toxins, impairing fisheries, recreational waters, and drinking water sources. HABs are often related to nutrient pollution, but nutrient reductions from surrounding watersheds require collaboration, awareness, and community buy-in to make sustainable long-term changes and prevent bloom formation. This is particularly the case for areas that have limited access to drinking water infrastructure and where the impacts of HABs have been largely overlooked. In this project, community-based activities engage two rural communities in Western Oregon near Tenmile Lakes and Dorena Lake with respect to HABs awareness, risks, and vulnerabilities. The communities’ economies are reliant on watershed resources, e.g., timber and agriculture, that may contribute to nutrient loading, and on resources provided by the impacted lake, such as fishing, drinking water, and irrigation water. In partnership with rural stakeholders, organizations, and community members, this project explores climate-smart, sustainable, value-added intervention strategies to prevent HABs and reduce health risks.

Collaborating with civic partners focused on environment and livelihood, our research addresses knowledge gaps regarding the health risks and economic impacts of cyanoHABs in rural regions. We work with local communities to address the loss of water security due to cyanoHABs and test the use of a carbon by-product technology, biochar, to mitigate impacts of cyanoHABs. Biochar is used in agriculture and forestry to improve soil and ecosystem health. Here we apply it in the context of watersheds and water treatment. Through roundtables, workshops, interviews, and pilot experiments, and in collaboration with civic partners, stakeholders, and impacted community members, our research assesses the efficacy, feasibility, and sustainability of local biochar (i) to enhance near shore buffer zones designed to mitigate nutrient loading and reduce frequency and severity of blooms and (ii) to remove cyanotoxins through gravity-fed filters. Our work informs mitigation and water treatment strategies in two rural communities and helps inform other projects in rural communities impacted by cyanoHABs globally.

This project is in response to the Civic Innovation Challenge program’s Track A. Climate and Environmental Instability - Building Resilient Communities through Co-Design, Adaption, and Mitigation and is a collaboration between NSF, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of Energy.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Background

Freshwater cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (cyanoHABs) represent a growing public health threat across the United States and globally. They damage local economies through fishery and recreation closures, and the toxins produced by cyanobacteria (cyanotoxins) can render drinking water unsafe. Effective water treatment requires rigorous monitoring, vigilant maintenance, and specialized expertise — challenges that strain even well-resourced municipalities. Rural communities are particularly vulnerable: small treatment plants and households drawing directly from affected surface or groundwater often lack adequate monitoring infrastructure. Many rural regions also depend on agriculture and timber, industries whose runoff contributes to the nutrient loading that drives bloom formation, creating tension among landowners, residents, and regulators. This project was centered at Tenmile Lakes, a rural watershed in western Oregon that relies on lake-based tourism and the timber economy and experiences annual cyanoHABs that frequently persist into late fall and early winter.

Project Overview and Goals

This Stage 1 planning grant investigated wood biochar — a potential value-added product from the timber industry — as a sustainable strategy to reduce nutrient loading, limit bloom formation, and remove cyanotoxins from drinking water. The project centered rural community needs around both livelihood and water quality, reconnecting watershed management to the broader landscape through participatory science. We collaborated with two civic partners: the Tenmile Lakes Basin Partnership (TLBP) and Aprovecho (d.b.a. Center for Rural Livelihoods, CRL). Together, we addressed the intersection of environmental degradation and economic decline in communities facing both water insecurity and the contraction of small-scale timber.

Research Activities and Findings

To assess the scalability, sustainability, and transferability of biochar for watershed application, the project conducted seven biochar production workshops (“burns”) engaging more than 120 participants, along with approximately 40 interviews across four sectors: the biochar industry, the timber sector, community and watershed groups, and rural residents. These activities connected constituencies interested in biochar production and use; explored pathways to promote adoption; assessed technical knowledge and experience; and identified barriers to widespread dissemination, particularly in rural settings.

Workshops addressed both technical considerations — including kiln size and design, labor requirements, vegetative feedstocks, and seasonal conditions — and cultural factors such as openness to novel approaches, fire competency, and interest in land-to-water stewardship. Participants had limited prior familiarity with biochar production methods but demonstrated strong interest and willingness to learn across all sectors. Water quality practitioners highlighted the multifactorial challenges posed by nonpoint source runoff in rural contexts and expressed need for concrete rural-scale application examples. Findings underscore the importance of building technical capacity, identifying cost-saving benefits and economic incentives, and fostering cultural change. These insights have directly informed CRL’s planning and have been shared with policymakers, relevant government agencies, interest groups, businesses, and community organizations.

At Tenmile Lakes, the project employed community-based participatory research — led through TLBP and its partners — to design a pilot field study investigating biochar applications for cyanoHAB prevention, mitigation, and treatment. The proposed study included in-situ interventions: construction and citizen-science-aided monitoring of biochar swales at key stormwater runoff sites; deployment of biochar “turtles” at high-use locations (near beaches and docks) during bloom events; and construction and testing of gravity-fed biochar filters alongside activated carbon filters. Several biochar roundtables co-hosted by TLBP and CRL examined small-scale production as well as biochar’s potential for carbon capture, waste reduction, and water quality improvement. Preliminary laboratory experiments assessed the efficacy of locally produced biochar filters in removing cyanotoxins from tap water.

Broader Impacts

The project contributed to interdisciplinary knowledge spanning water quality, public health, forestry, rural governance, and climate science, and advances NSF priorities in translational research by collecting data and modeling community engagement methods applicable to civic water engineering, public health communication, and watershed management. The project supported STEM education and workforce development through participation of high school students in biochar workshops; training of five undergraduate researchers in community engagement and laboratory methods; and mentorship of two female scientists. Incorporation of project themes into pre-health sciences curricula further extended educational reach. The participatory structure — built around civic partnerships — increased public scientific literacy and strengthened connections among academic researchers, business owners, watershed and forestry managers, community organizations, and rural residents.

The results have broader implications for national priorities, including wildfire risk reduction and rural water infrastructure security. The project identified specific avenues for — and barriers to — integrating biochar into rural timber economies as a value-added product. The engagement strategies developed here offer a replicable model for building transparency and trust among public health agencies, watershed stakeholders, and rural populations, enabling the cultural change necessary for adoption of practices that benefit ecosystems, human health, and local economies through improved water quality, reduced air pollution, reduced wildfire risk, and more sustainable management of timber waste.
